item.title: Attorney General Bonta Secures Third Legal Victory in One Week Against Trump Administration’s Attempt to Interfere in California Elections
item.description:
October 30, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today secured another victory in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, marking his office’s third legal victory in one week in the fight to protect California’s elections from the Trump Administration’s interference. The ruling is the latest setback for the federal government’s effort to force California election officials to segregate and not count any mail-in ballots that may be returned by a list of approximately 20,000 individuals it “believes” are “likely” noncitizens.  A court ruling earlier this week found that the Trump Administration’s “methodology in creating the list was vague and raised multiple questions regarding reliability,” and that “district courts across the country have cast doubt about the United States’ proffered lists.”

“Three legal victories in one week make clear that the Trump Administration has zero authority to interfere in California’s elections,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta. “California law makes it illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and there are several state laws that guard against it. That is why it is exceptionally rare. The Administration’s baseless claims of widespread fraud are an attempt to sow doubt in our democratic process and risk disenfranchising eligible voters. We will keep fighting to uphold the rule of law.”

“Trump and his administration just lost for the third time this week in their desperate and dangerous attempts to meddle in the California election process with voting already underway and just days before Election Day. These attacks on our democracy are serious, and the full force of our state is defending our democracy right now,” said Governor Gavin Newsom. “We will continue to fight them on their illegal power grabs every step of the way, and deliver a free and fair election just as we’ve always done.”

Attorney General Bonta filed his opposition this morning before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals to the Trump Administration’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal, arguing that the court should reject the federal government’s request because: 

  • The Purcell principle protects against last-minute election changes: The Purcell principle prohibits court-ordered changes to election rules close to an election when they threaten to confuse voters and disrupt election administration.
  • The Administration is unlikely to succeed on the merits: The U.S. Constitution gives States and Congress — not the President or the Executive Branch — the authority to regulate the time, place, and manner of elections.
  • Equitable considerations weigh heavily against granting the Administration’s request: Granting the Administration’s request would undermine States’ authority to run their elections and place unnecessary burdens on election officials and voters.

Today’s win follows two legal victories for California earlier this week: on Monday, October 26, the Ninth Circuit dismissed the federal government’s first appeal because it had not given the district court adequate time to consider its request; on Wednesday, October 28, the district court denied the federal government’s request for a temporary restraining order.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Files Felony Charges Against Former Lassen Superior Court Executive Officer
item.description:
October 29, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced felony charges against a former Lassen Superior Court Executive Officer for allegedly misappropriating more than $14,000 in public funds. Between 2022 and 2025, the former executive officer allegedly used a court-issued credit card and submitted falsified reimbursement requests to cover personal expenses.

“Public officials have a responsibility to safeguard taxpayer dollars. When those who are trusted with public funds misuse them for personal gain, they will be held accountable,” said Attorney General Bonta. “My office will continue to investigate and prosecute public corruption to protect the integrity of our institutions and the Californians they serve.”

In October 2024, Lassen Superior Court employees identified questionable transactions involving court-issued credit and fuel cards. The concerns were reported to the court’s presiding judge, who subsequently notified the LassenCounty Sheriff’s Office. In July 2025, at the request of the Lassen County District Attorney’s Office, the California Department of Justice assumed responsibility for completing the investigation. Investigators reviewed court financial records, reimbursement requests, and internal purchasing procedures and interviewed witnesses. The investigation identified approximately $14,285 in allegedly unauthorized expenditures involving personal purchase and reimbursement requests.

It is important to note that charges are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Joins Amicus Brief Supporting State's Right to Seek Accountability for Fraud Among Private Businesses
item.description:
October 29, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta, as part of a coalition of 17 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in People of the State of New York v. Trump, emphasizing the important role state attorneys general play in policing economic fraud even when that fraud takes place in private commercial transactions between sophisticated parties. New York law authorizes the New York Attorney General to seek judicial remedies for repeated or persistent business fraud or illegality. In today’s amicus brief, the coalition urges the New York Court of Appeals to uphold a lower court’s ruling that the New York Attorney General had authority under this law to bring an action against Donald Trump and other defendants for fraud against sophisticated business entities that declined to pursue the legal remedies available to them.

“Fraud is fraud, and it should be treated as such,” said Attorney General Bonta. “There is no loophole that allows for corrupt business practices, and there is no technicality that prevents the state from upholding antifraud laws. As attorneys general, it is our job as the top law enforcement officers to root out any and all corruption in our states' economies. We urge the New York Court of Appeals to see this case for what it is and affirm the New York Attorney General’s authority to prosecute all fraudulent business dealings that occur in the state, regardless of the parties involved.” 

In 2022, the New York Attorney General sued Donald Trump and other defendants for engaging in financial fraud by inflating Trump’s statements of financial condition in submissions to lenders and others for the purpose of obtaining favorable business deals. The trial court held Trump and other defendants liable for fraud. This liability finding was upheld on appeal, and the matter is now on appeal before New York’s highest court.

In the amicus brief, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition assert that:

  • States have a sovereign interest in eradicating all kinds of fraud from their economies and retain extensive police powers to protect against fraud.
  • Many states’ attorneys general have broad authority to enforce antifraud laws, even when fraud occurs between sophisticated private parties who decline to pursue their own remedies.
  • States’ enforcement of antifraud laws in these contexts serves the public interest, protecting the interests of stakeholders who lack the practical ability to act, leveling the playing field for others who must compete with those who are willing to commit and benefit from fraud, and protecting the public from the damage that fraud can cause to competitive markets and to public safety.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Oregon, Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

item.title: Privacy Rights Can’t Be Left in the Rearview: Attorney General Bonta Secures $1.8 Million Settlement with Lyft
item.description:
October 29, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced a settlement with Lyft, resolving allegations that the company violated the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and California’s Unfair Competition Law by failing to offer consumers the ability to opt out of the sale of their personal information within Lyft’s mobile app. The settlement includes $1.8 million in civil penalties and requires Lyft to provide an in-app opt-out option and notify California consumers of their right to not have their personal information sold.

“Lyft — a company that offers its services exclusively through an app — was selling and sharing user’s personal information for targeted advertising without giving users a way to opt-out from within that app. Instead, consumers had to detour through a privacy policy, re-enter personal information, and transfer from the app to webpage just to exercise a right the law guarantees them. This is cumbersome and confusing — and in California, it’s illegal,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Under California’s nation-leading privacy law, consumers have the right to say no to the sale and sharing of their data, and businesses cannot throw up unnecessary roadblocks.” 

Attorney General Bonta's settlement with Lyft stems from a March 2025 investigative sweep concerning how companies use geolocation data, including in the context of selling or sharing consumers' personal information. In order to use Lyft, consumers — both riders and drivers — must download the Lyft app and create an account. Lyft then collects and uses personal information like name, email address, or phone number; IP addresses; and non-precise geolocation, such as city, state, region, or zip code. Since mid-2023, Lyft has also been selling or sharing consumers’ personal information to target and display ads within the Lyft app but did not provide an in-app opt-out method. Instead, the only way for a consumer to opt out was to navigate through a series of links from Lyft’s in-app Privacy Policy to access Lyft’s “Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information” webpage, a cumbersome process that does not satisfy the CCPA’s requirements. And while Lyft knew the identity of consumers who submitted requests through this form because it required them to log in to use its app, Lyft still required consumers to re-enter their log in and submit further personal information to exercise their right to opt out. This was an illegal and unnecessary barrier to the exercise of CCPA rights. 

In addition to $1.8 million in civil penalties, the settlement requires Lyft to provide an in-app opt-out option and notify California consumers of their right to not have their personal information sold.

California Consumer Privacy Act

The CCPA vests California consumers with control over the personal information that businesses collect about them, including the right to request that businesses stop selling or sharing their personal information. Learn more about opting out. 

Attorney General Bonta is committed to the robust enforcement of California’s nation-leading privacy law. Today’s settlement represents the California Department of Justice's ninth enforcement action under the CCPA. Attorney General Bonta has also announced settlements with General Motors, Sephora, DoorDash, and Disney as well as mobile app gaming company, Jam City; streaming service, Sling TV; website publisher, Healthline.com; and entertainment company, Tilting Point Media.

For more information about the CCPA, visit oag.ca.gov/ccpa. To report a violation of the CCPA to the Attorney General, consumers can submit a complaint online at oag.ca.gov/report.

Stop, DROP, and Secure Your Data

Californians can now send one request to more than 575 registered data brokers to delete their personal data using a new, easy-to-use online tool. The Delete Request and Opt-out Platform (DROP), developed by CalPrivacy, gives Californians more control over their personal information and helps limit the information that data brokers sell. Formore information about DROP and how Californians can submit a deletion request, visit: privacy.ca.gov/drop.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Defends State Gambling Laws Against Kalshi
item.description:
October 29, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

Joins bipartisan coalition for the ninth time 

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today joined a bipartisan coalition of 37 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief supporting Utah’s right to enforce its state sports gaming and gambling laws against prediction market operator Kalshi. The amicus brief supports Utah gaming authorities in KalshiEX LLC v. Cox, which is pending in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit. The attorneys general primarily argue that federal preemption of state gambling laws as applied to prediction market providers is improper and detrimental to the traditional role of the state to regulate gambling and protect vulnerable citizens. This filing marks the ninth time California has joined nationwide multistate amicus efforts targeting Kalshi and similar prediction market companies.

"This filing is representative of our bipartisan commitment to protecting state regulatory authority over illegal, unregulated gambling operations," said Attorney General Bonta. “Prediction markets cannot use federal loopholes to bypass state consumer protection, sports gaming, and gambling laws. By joining this brief, we are standing firmly with Utah and our state partners to ensure that federal commodities laws are not weaponized to evade state laws, fuel gambling addiction, and undermine state regulation of legal gaming."

Kalshi’s appeal requests the Tenth Circuit find that the federal Commodities Exchange Act preempts Utah’s state constitutional prohibition on sports wagering as applied to the sports event contracts traded on prediction market providers like Kalshi. In the brief, the attorneys general primarily argue that federal preemption of state gambling laws as applied to prediction market providers is improper and detrimental to the traditional role of the states in regulating gambling and protecting vulnerable citizens. The brief is comparable to others filed in similar cases nationwide, including in the Third, Fourth, Sixth, and Ninth Circuits, and in support of New Jersey’s Petition for Writ Certiorari to the United States Supreme Court. 

Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai'i, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nebraska, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming in filing the breif.

Here is a copy of the brief.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Sues Trump Administration to Defend State Law Prohibiting the Sale of Non-Reusable Propane Cylinders
item.description:
October 29, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today filed a lawsuit challenging the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration’s (PHMSA) administrative determination that California Senate Bill (SB) 1280 is preempted by the Hazardous Materials Transportation Act (HMTA). SB 1280, authored by Senator John Laird (D–Santa Cruz), prohibits, with limited exceptions, the sale in California of certain non-reusable and non-fillable propane cylinders beginning on January 1, 2028. Propane cylinders are single-use, generally one-pound containers used in applications like camping stoves, portable heaters, and lanterns. When disposed into the waste stream, they pose a significant explosion and fire risk, environmental and health impacts, and a costly burden on local governments to safely manage. The purpose of California’s law is to reduce the volume of propane cylinders that are being improperly disposed of in the municipal waste stream and that threaten environmental harm and the safety of waste pickup, landfill, and recycling workers. In today’s lawsuit, Attorney General Bonta is petitioning for judicial review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to vacate the administrative determination. 

“Once again, the Trump Administration is trying to overrule California’s laws aimed at protecting public safety, health, and the environment,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta. “Let’s be clear about what this law does: It will protect workers and the environment from residual propane explosions and save local governments millions of tax dollars in waste management costs. We’ll continue to fight against the Administration’s federal overreach armed with the law and facts on our side.” 

“I thank Attorney General Bonta for taking on the Trump Administration’s federal overreach. I authored SB 1280 to save taxpayers the cost of disposing of used propane canisters, and to protect workers and communities from the fire and explosion risks posed by propane cylinders thrown away in our parks and beaches,” said Senator John Laird (D–Santa Cruz). “Let’s be clear: this law doesn’t ban propane. It simply replaces dangerous single-use cylinders with refillable alternatives. Yet the Trump Administration would rather protect a company’s business model than the safety of California workers and taxpayers. Our responsibility is to protect Californians and our environment.”

The federal HMTA establishes a national regulatory scheme for the safe transportation of hazardous materials and authorizes the Department of Transportation to adopt regulations designating hazardous materials and specifying the design of hazardous materials packaging and containers. The Department of Transportation, through PHMSA, has adopted the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR), which designate propane as a hazardous material and prescribe design specifications for compressed-gas cylinders. Although propane cylinders are required to be disposed of as hazardous waste, an estimated 3 million of the estimated 4 million one-pound, single-use propane cylinders sold in California each year are placed into municipal waste streams. These cylinders often contain residual gas of which the user is unaware. When damaged or crushed in a waste hauling truck, sorting facility, landfill, or recycling facility, residual gas may explode or catch fire, causing injury. 

On January 9, 2026, PHMSA published a notice that Worthington Enterprises, Inc., an Ohio-based manufacturer of disposable propane cylinders, had asked PHMSA to determine that HMTA preempts SB 1280. The Attorney General submitted a comment letter defending SB 1280. On September 10, 2026, PHMSA published its determination on Worthington’s preemption application. PHMSA determined that SB 1280 is preempted because it imposes requirements that are “not substantively the same” as cylinder designs prescribed by HMR and because it stands as an obstacle to HMTA’s purposes. However, SB 1280 is not preempted under HMTA because HMR authorizes refillable propane cylinders and refillable cylinders, which are widely available for sale, and SB 1280 does not regulate the transportation of disposable propane cylinders. Today’s suit asks the Court to recognize that HMTA and HMR do not preempt SB 1280 and strike down PHMSA’s preemption determination.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Supports State Laws Ensuring Minors Receive Protection and Medical Care
item.description:
October 29, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta yesterday joined a coalition of 18 attorneys general in submitting an amicus brief in International Partners for Ethical Care, Inc. v Ferguson, relating to Washington State’s laws surrounding runaway minors who seek refuge and care at licensed youth homeless shelters. In the brief, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition argue that the collection of parents challenging these laws lacks proper legal standing to make their challenge in court. Attorney General Bonta and the coalition also highlight that the lawsuit would create preferential treatment for certain constitutional rights over others, and harms states’ legitimate interest to protect the health of their residents. 

“Minors fleeing from difficult home lives deserve to receive proper protection and access to crucial medical treatment,” said Attorney General Bonta. “State laws like those in Washington allow licensed youth homeless shelters to care for minors seeking refuge while acknowledging the important role parents play in their children’s lives. These laws are being challenged by individuals who have no direct stake in, and who are unaffected by, the challenged laws. California remains committed to safeguarding our youths’ physical and mental well-being while respecting parents’ rights. We will continue to work to empower healthy parent-child relationships and ensure all individuals facing difficult times receive support to help them thrive.”

In November 2023, a collection of parents sued Washington in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, asserting that Washington’s laws governing parental notification when a minor seeks refuge at a licensed youth homeless shelter — Wash. Rev. Code § 71.34.530, Engrossed Senate Bill 5599, and Substitute House Bill 1406 — violate the coalition’s Constitutional rights by interfering with their ability to parent. The district court dismissed the coalition’s complaint, and when the coalition appealed, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court’s ruling. The case is now being considered by the U.S. Supreme Court. 

In the amicus brief, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition urge the Supreme Court to once again affirm the district court’s dismissal of the lawsuit. Attorney General Bonta and the coalition argue that:

  • The suing parents have not provided adequate evidence to demonstrate that their complaint has legitimate legal standing.
  • The parents’ complaint, if accepted, would constitute an exception to legal precedent that leads to parental rights being given preferential treatment over other Constitutional rights.
  • The lawsuit threatens states’ legitimate interest to protect the well-being of their child residents. 

In filing the amicus brief, Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Massachusetts, Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Vermont.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Secures Major Victory Blocking Implementation of Unlawful Medicaid Work Requirements for Medically Frail Individuals
item.description:
October 29, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today secured a decision by the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts finding the Trump Administration’s implementation of new Medicaid work requirements under the Big Beautiful Bill Act unlawful. In a lawsuit filed in June 2026, Attorney General Bonta and a multistate coalition challenged provisions of an interim final rule, which adopted a new interpretation of key terms like “medically frail,” making it harder for medically vulnerable individuals to be excused from the work requirements. In today’s decision, the District Court held that the Trump Administration’s definition of “medical frailty” is contrary to law, vacated the language, issued a permanent injunction, and granted the plaintiff states’ a six-month stay of enforcement to accommodate any errors or delays resulting from the necessary changes to implementation. 

“Today’s decision is a major victory that ensures that some of our most vulnerable residents are able to continue to access the healthcare they deserve,” said Attorney General Bonta. “People with serious illnesses or disabilities should not have to worry about losing their healthcare because of work requirements or related barriers. That’s not what Congress intended, and despite the Trump Administration’s cruel attempts to rip away healthcare from those in need, that’s not what the court held today. I’m proud to fight for affordable healthcare for all our states’ residents.”

BACKGROUND

Medicaid is the nation’s safety net healthcare program for low-income Americans and is jointly funded by states and the federal government, with the federal government providing at least 50% of the cost of services. Congress created exemptions from Medicaid’s work requirements to ensure that people with serious illnesses and disabilities do not lose coverage or face interruptions in care. 

Yet despite months of working with states on implementation, earlier this year, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) surprised states with an interim final rule that makes it harder for medically vulnerable individuals to be excused from the work requirements and makes other changes that increase administrative burdens, create unnecessary red tape, and put eligible people at risk of losing their health coverage — including those who are already working or qualify for an exemption. The rule disregarded substantial evidence that should have been considered, failed to adequately evaluate reasonable alternatives, and did not give states clear or workable guidance. 

Past Medicaid work requirement programs have shown that added red tape causes eligible people to lose coverage, placing greater strain on state Medicaid programs, safety net providers, and emergency rooms, while increasing costs as more medically frail residents become uninsured.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Secures District Court Victory Denying Trump Administration’s TRO, Building on Earlier Appellate Win to Protect California Elections
item.description:
October 28, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today issued the following statement after the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California denied the Trump Administration’s request for a temporary restraining order (TRO) that would have required California election officials to segregate and not count mail-in ballots returned by approximately 20,000 individuals the administration “believes” are “likely” noncitizens, but has also admitted could include several U.S. citizens. Attorney General Bonta filed a brief opposing the TRO, a supplemental brief further opposing the TRO, and a motion to dismiss the federal government’s lawsuit. Today’s district court victory builds on Monday’s win at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which rejected the administration’s attempt to obtain emergency relief by bypassing the district court.

“No administration can disenfranchise thousands of individuals or disrupt an ongoing election based on highly unreliable claims of noncitizenship,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta. “Today’s ruling is yet another important victory for the rule of law and the right to vote. But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California’s elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed.”

“For the second day this week, our country’s legal system is standing up to the President’s authoritarian attempts to remain in power unchecked and unchallenged. For more than a year, California’s sovereignty has been under siege, and this lawsuit is his latest attack on the rule of law, the California Constitution, and the U.S. Constitution,” said Governor Gavin Newsom. “California will continue to deliver a free and fair election that follows both state and federal law, as the Judicial Branch — importantly a co-equal branch of government — is deciding in real time, much to the Trump Administration’s dismay.”

In opposing the administration’s request for a TRO, Attorney General Bonta argued that the court should deny the request because it would:

  • Lack a legal basis: The administration has no legal basis to force California to segregate and not count ballots based on unverified claims about citizenship.
  • Risk disenfranchising eligible voters: The administration’s list could include eligible voters, and the administration has not provided California with the underlying data and methodology needed to evaluate its validity.
  • Violate federal and state law: The administration’s demands would conflict with federal laws protecting voting rights and California laws governing elections.
  • Disrupt an ongoing election: Requiring California to change its ballot-counting procedures in the middle of an election would disrupt the election and create unnecessary confusion for election officials and voters.

The district court agreed with all those arguments, decisively rejecting the federal government’s motion.

In the order, the court observed that “[e]roded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.” And it explained that “[p]oll taxes, literacy tests, and other obstacles [have been] used to prevent individuals from casting their vote. Every generation in our history has witnessed repeated clashes between those who seek to limit access to the ballot and those who fight to ensure it. In this case, the federal government seeks to segregate and exclude over 20,000 ballots. This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections. If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve. The Government’s Application for Temporary Restraining Order is DENIED.”

The Trump Administration’s latest attempt to interfere in California’s elections follows years of efforts to undermine election results and voting rights:

  • After losing the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden, President Trump pressured Georgia officials to “find” 11,780 votes, fueled the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol as Congress certified Biden’s victory, and continues to falsely claim that he won the 2020 presidential election — even seizing ballots from that election in Fulton County, Georgia, in January 2026 as part of efforts to relitigate the results.
  • The Trump Administration sought to impose new restrictions on voting and election administration through executive orders that courts have found unlawful, including the recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling led by Attorney General Bonta blocking the administration’s attempts to seize control of mail voting nationwide.
  • In July 2026, the Trump Administration initially alleged that California had more than 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls, which the Trump Administration reduced to about 20,000 — a 90% decrease from their earlier allegations — before bringing this litigation. This mirrors the Trump Administration’s accusations against Nevada, where the Trump Administration initially claimed that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizen voters. It later reduced that number to 185 voters and has not provided evidence to support its claim that all of the 185 individuals are noncitizens.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta: States Must Have the Ability to Protect Residents from Assault Rifles Commonly Used in Mass Shootings
item.description:
October 28, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND —  California Attorney General Rob Bonta today, as part of a coalition of 19 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Supreme Court in support of laws enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, restricting the sale, manufacture, and possession of certain uniquely dangerous assault rifles. The brief, filed in Viramontes v. County of Cook, urges the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold appellate court rulings that affirmed that these challenged assault weapon laws are consistent with the Second Amendment and the nation’s strong historical tradition of regulating weapons that are uniquely dangerous.

“The California Department of Justice will continue to aggressively defend life-saving safety measures and support local leaders with the tools necessary to keep people safe. Assault weapon laws restrict a small and uniquely dangerous category of weapons that have proven to be mass shooters’ weapon of choice for a reason,” said Attorney General Bonta. “California enacted the nation’s first state-level assault weapons restriction almost four decades ago to protect our residents from uniquely dangerous weapons with battlefield features that facilitate indiscriminate mass killing. The Supreme Court has the opportunity to affirm what many appellate courts have already found: these commonsense protections are reasonable and constitutional. A mass shooter with an assault weapon demonstrably can inflict more deaths and injuries compared to those using other weapons, and three-quarters of mass shootings of 10 or more victims from 2012 to 2022 involved the use of an assault weapon. Protecting our communities from mass shootings and gun violence is a core responsibility of state and local government.”

The coalition’s amicus brief explains that the AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are uniquely dangerous because their features facilitate assaultive mass killing and are poorly designed for self-defense purposes. The brief also explains that the U.S. has a long historical tradition of regulating uniquely dangerous weapons. It also urges the Supreme Court to reject petitioners’ argument that the Second Amendment prohibits laws restricting any weapon, regardless of dangerousness, once it has reached some arbitrary popularity threshold. The brief argues this would be a dangerous, illogical, and ahistorical outcome that is contrary to the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment caselaw , and would also encourage firearms manufacturers to flood communities with new dangerous weapons before a legislature manages to institute restrictions to prevent them from proliferating in shootings and other criminal activity.

California has been a leader among states that have enacted effective firearm safety laws. Republican Governor George Deukmejian signed California’s initial bipartisan assault weapons restriction into law in 1989 following a hate-motivated school shooting at Cleveland Elementary School in Stockton, California, in which a gunman wielding an AK 47-style semiautomatic assault rifle with detachable 30-round and 75-round large-capacity magazines fired over 100 times in about three minutes — murdering five young children and injuring 30 other students and a teacher. A 2026 report from the California Department of Justice's Office of Gun Violence Prevention showed that California’s mass shooting victimization rate for 2023-2025 fell to 38% below the rate for the rest of the U.S. on average. Today, 10 other states and several cities generally restrict the sale, manufacture, and possession of assault rifles, including the AK-47 and AR-15. 

Connecticut enacted its initial assault weapons law in 1993 and expanded that law in 2013 following the December 2012 Sandy Hook elementary school shooting in which a gunman armed with an AR-15 style rifle and large capacity magazines fired over 150 rounds and murdered 20 children and six educators in under five minutes. 

Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington s in filing the brief.

A copy of the brief can be found here.
